name: Alcuin of York
knownFor: Master of the school at York who taught Charlemagne and ended his life as abbot of Saint Martin's at Tours. He wrote against Felix of Urgel and Elipandus of Toledo over the teaching that Christ in his human nature was God's adopted Son.
dates: No source used here gives the year of his birth. Jean Mabillon dates his meeting with Charlemagne at Parma to 780 and his abbacy at Tours to 796. The older Life that Mabillon follows puts his death in May 804, and a short Tours chronicle gives 804. Mabillon argues that he lived on past 810
place: The province of York, where Mabillon says he was born; York, where he was raised and taught; Charlemagne's court in Francia; Tours, where he was abbot of Saint Martin's and was buried
role: Deacon; master of the school at York; teacher at Charlemagne's court; abbot of Saint Martin's at Tours; theologian and poet

keyWorks.title: On the Faith of the Holy and Undivided Trinity, three books
keyWorks.about: written for Charlemagne. Froben, abbot of Saint Emmeram, whose edition Migne reprints, places it at Tours near the end of Alcuin's life and dates it to 802. Thegan, sending it to a bishop, calls it what the holy Alcuin, the greatest of scholars, gathered from many books of Augustine

keyWorks.title: Against Felix, seven books, and Against Elipandus, four books
keyWorks.about: his answers to the teaching that Christ in his human nature is God's adopted Son. He says the seven books were read and approved before the king and his priests. Against Elipandus he answers the warning that he must not corrupt the king

keyWorks.title: Poem on the bishops and saints of the church of York
keyWorks.about: a long poem on York's bishops and saints. It tells how Bishop Ælberht left the see to Eanbald and his books to another pupil. It lists the authors those books held, from Jerome and Augustine to Bede, Boethius and Aristotle

traces: Altfrid's Life of Liudger tells that Liudger studied under Alcuin at York for three years and six months, and came home with many books.
Rabanus, his pupil, entered him in his calendar of saints under 19 May with the words "Depositio domni Alcuini", Mabillon reports.
Thegan sent the books on the Trinity to a bishop Hatto, Froben notes. Aeneas, bishop of Paris, quotes them in his book against the Greeks.
Alcuin wrote verses for the church that Liudger built where Boniface of Mainz and his companions were killed. Altfrid gives them in his Life of Liudger.
In verses to the bishop and monks of Lindisfarne, Alcuin mourned the day a pagan band came suddenly by ship to the shore. He urged them not to let the trial break their minds.
remembered: Einhard, as Mabillon quotes him, calls Alcuin a deacon from Britain, of Saxon race, the most learned man anywhere.

The Annals of Fulda, as Mabillon quotes them, say under 794 that Alcuin, also called Albinus, was famed for holiness and learning. Ardo, in his Life of Benedict of Aniane, calls him renowned for wisdom and venerable for holiness.
Mabillon says the founding of the University of Paris was later credited to him, since he had been head of the palace schools. As far as Mabillon knows, no church kept his feast day, not even Tours.

uncertain: His life rests largely on Jean Mabillon's seventeenth-century essay. Mabillon draws on an older Life, whose writer he calls nearly a contemporary, and which is not among the sources used here. Nor are Alcuin's letters, apart from the passages Mabillon quotes.

His death. The older Life, as Mabillon reports it, gives May 804, and a short Tours chronicle gives 804. Mabillon keeps the day and argues for a later year, past 810. He points to verses on Saint Amand dated 809 and to Rabanus's books on the Cross. Froben dates the books on the Trinity to 802, near the end of Alcuin's life. The day itself reads xiv before the Kalends of June, that is 19 May, in two places in this scan, and xvi in one.

His brother. Mabillon says he had a brother Aquila, bishop of Salzburg, on the strength of a letter addressed to his dearest brother Aquila, a bishop. Mabillon identifies this Aquila with Arno of Salzburg.

The Saxons. Mabillon says letters of Alcuin show what he thought of easing the tithes Charlemagne wanted from the newly baptized Saxons. Those letters are not among the sources used here, and neither is his line that faith is a matter of the will.

The poem on York. Mabillon called its author anonymous. Thomas Gale printed it under Alcuin's name in 1691. Oudin gave it to Fridegod, and the Maurist Rivet answered him. The prefatory note in Froben's edition sides with Rivet.

His years in Francia. Mabillon reckons that Alcuin went home to England about 790 and came back about three years later, to answer Elipandus and Felix. The Frankfurt decree of 794 asks the council to receive him into its fellowship. Alfred Boretius notes that he attended it as an envoy from Britain.
His wealth. Mabillon reports Elipandus's charge that Alcuin had twenty thousand slaves, and answers that he held his abbeys to reform their monks.
His name. Mabillon separates four men called Albinus, among them an abbot at Canterbury whom Cardinal Baronius took for Alcuin.
